		const mnjsEndpoint = 'https://warp.media.net/js/tags/clientag.js?'
		+ 'cid=' + window.mnjs.customerId
		+ '&dn=' + window.mnjs.domain
		+ '&version=' + window.mnjs.version;
		loadScript(mnjsEndpoint);
	};

	/**
	 * gets user agent from navigator info
	 * @param {String} ua user agent from navigator
	 * @param {String} isMobileAndroid for android devices
	 * @param {String} isMobileWindows for windows phone devices
	 * @returns a string representing the user agent
	 */
	const getIsMobile = (ua, isMobileAndroid, isMobileWindows) => ua.match(/iP(hone|od)/i)
		|| ua.match(/iPod/i)
		|| ua.match(/BlackBerry/i)
		|| isMobileAndroid
		|| isMobileWindows;

	const ua = navigator.userAgent;
	const isMobileAndroid = ua.match(/Android/i) && ua.match(/Mobile/i);
	const isMobileWindows = ua.match(/Nokia|NOKIA/i) && ua.match(/Symbian|Windows Phone/i);
	const isMobile = getIsMobile(ua, isMobileAndroid, isMobileWindows);

	const loadMedianetHeaderBidding = () => {
		if (window.forbes.isAdvisor) {
		loadScript('https://contextual.media.net/bidexchange.js?cid=8CU25AH4U');
		} else {
		loadMedianetManagePrebid(isMobile);
		}
	};

	const loadMedianetAd = () => {
		const { lastCustomData } = window.forbes;
		// mnet ad logic here https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1kI9tKGs1jhu9j4J-RqFKz-TRhxiH3lY-He62on7qkLg/edit#gid=917757669
		const brandVoice = ((lastCustomData?.contribType && lastCustomData.contribType === 'AdVoice') || (lastCustomData?.author && lastCustomData.author === 'AdVoice'));
		const pageType = window.forbes['simple-site']?.adZone;
		const unpaidContribType = (pageType === 'contribhome' && !brandVoice);
		// mnet exists on legacy paid content types
		const legacyPaidContent = lastCustomData['Paid Content'] && !brandVoice;
		// this returns a string 'true' or 'false'
		const premiumProfile = window.forbes['simple-site']?.tracking?.premiumProfiles;
		const isChanSec = ['channel', 'section'].includes(pageType);
		const isBasicProfile = pageType === 'profile' && (premiumProfile === 'false');
		const isHome = window.mnjs?.channel?.includes('home');
		const isTopics = window.location.pathname.includes('/topics/');
		// only load the mnet ad where it's rendered
		// search and article on both DT and mobile (not vetted, paid content or premium)
		const search = window.location.pathname.includes('search');
		const article = (!brandVoice && (['live', 'topline', 'standard', 'advisor', 'finds'].includes(window.templateType) || pageType.includes('article/standard') || pageType.includes('article-blue/standard'))) || pageType.includes('masthead') || legacyPaidContent;
		// mobile specific to home, video page, video standalone, unpaid contrib, unpaid profile, and chansec
		const requireMobileMnet = isMobile && !brandVoice && ((window.location.pathname.includes('video') || unpaidContribType || isChanSec || isBasicProfile || isHome || legacyPaidContent || isTopics));
		if (search || article || requireMobileMnet) {
		loadScript('https://contextual.media.net/dmedianet.js?cid=8CU2T3HV4&https=1');
		}
	};

	/**
	 * check if the _swb_consent_ cookie is loaded
	 * @Todo make the ketch checks on the window so we can call them from there and make sure we dont
	 * lose time in the proccess
	 * we added ketch check to make sure we don't load medianet if the user is in the EU or China
	 * adding the checks here is a temporary solution.
	 * @returns boolean that represents if the cookie is loaded or not
	 */
	const checkConsentCookieLoaded = () => !!document.cookie.match(/_swb_consent_=/);

	/**
	 * get the _swb_consent_ cookie and url decode it to get it ready for parseing
	 * @returns String that has the ketch cookie value
	 */
	function getSwbCookieValue() {
		let cookieValue = false;
		if (!checkConsentCookieLoaded()) {
		return cookieValue;
		}

		const ketchCookieName = '_swb_consent_=';
		document.cookie.split(';').forEach((cookie) => {
		if (cookie.trim().startsWith(ketchCookieName)) {
		cookieValue = decodeURIComponent(cookie.split('=')[1]);
		}
		});

		return cookieValue;
	}

	/**
	 * get the cookie and parse it into json from base64 string
	 * @returns object that contains the consent details
	 */
	function getSwbCookie() {
		const ketchCookie = getSwbCookieValue();

		try {
		const cookieInfo = window.atob(ketchCookie);
		return JSON.parse(cookieInfo);
		} catch (error) {
		return {};
		}
	}

	/**
	 * Check if the user gave full consent.
	 * @returns If the user gave full consent.
	 */
	function userGaveFullConsent() {
		const userConsent = getSwbCookie();

		if (!userConsent.purposes) {
		return false;
		}

		const purposesKeys = Object.keys(userConsent.purposes);
		let userConsentPrefrences = true;

		// safety check for when the cookie is first intialized
		if (purposesKeys.length === 1) {
		return false;
		}

		purposesKeys.forEach((element) => {
		if (userConsent.purposes[element].allowed === 'false') {
		userConsentPrefrences = false;
		}
		});

		return userConsentPrefrences;
	}

	function waitForWindowObject(ss, lcd) {
		return new Promise((resolve) => {
		function checkObject() {
		if (window.forbes[ss] && window.forbes[lcd]) {
		resolve();
		} else {
		setTimeout(checkObject, 1000);
		}
		}
		checkObject();
		});
	}

	if (window.forbes.isEurope || window.forbes.isChina) {
		if (checkConsentCookieLoaded() && userGaveFullConsent()) {
		loadMedianetHeaderBidding();
		waitForWindowObject('simple-site', 'lastCustomData').then(loadMedianetAd);
		}
	} else {
		loadMedianetHeaderBidding();
		waitForWindowObject('simple-site', 'lastCustomData').then(loadMedianetAd);
	}
})();

style="--lsts-accent-primary: #5C64D1"><div data-theme="light"><div class="IntroBlock-module_headingContent__-BZfw list-lander-intro"><div class="IntroBlock-module_introText__uqCeW"><div class="list-lander-p">More than two years after <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/alexkonrad/2023/02/02/inside-chatggpts-breakout-moment-and-the-race-for-the-future-of-ai">the blockbuster launch of ChatGPT</a>, artificial intelligence continues to be the white hot center of venture capital and the business world at large. Some of the buzziest startups have shifted focus from the AI model release horserace to building useful applications and products on top of existing models, automating scutwork across fields like engineering, healthcare, legal and sales. That’s evident in <i>Forbes’</i> seventh annual AI 50 list, produced in partnership with Sequoia and Meritech Capital, which spotlights the most promising privately-held AI companies in the world.   </div><div class="list-lander-p"></div><div class="list-lander-p">Newcomers to the list include $2.5 billion-valued <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2024/08/22/engineers-at-openai-and-midjourney-are-using-this-400-million-startups-ai-coding-software/">Anysphere</a> (better known as Cursor), a three year-old AI startup that helps engineers write and edit code and has at least $100 million in annualized revenue; the $1 billion-valued AI language tutor app Speak, which is used by some 10 million people to learn English and Spanish; and Massachusetts-based unicorn OpenEvidence, which is building an AI-powered search platform that summarizes medical information for doctors. </div><div class="list-lander-p"></div><div class="list-lander-p">Model builders like OpenAI and Anthropic remain the biggest companies on the list, having raised large sums of cash from marquee Silicon Valley venture capitalists. The two AI behemoths have accumulated a combined $81 billion in venture funding, more than half of the total $142.45 billion that companies on this year’s AI 50 list have raised. But this year, there’s also a hefty new competition from Elon Musk’s xAI ($12.1 billion in funding) and former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati’s stealthy startup Thinking Machine Labs, which is developing broadly capable  AI systems and <a href="https://www.businessinsider.com/mira-murati-new-startup-thinking-machine-labs-valuation-2025-2">reportedly</a> raising $1 billion at a valuation of about $9 billion. Meanwhile, Fei Fei Li, known as the “godmother of AI”, has launched her own startup too, World Labs ($291.5 million raised), to develop models that can understand physical spaces. And then there’s enterprise AI company Writer ($326 million raised), which is training its own models to handle mundane business tasks like writing marketing blogs and searching through troves of documents. (Read our feature story on Writer <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2025/04/10/why-300-companies-use-this-startups-ai-to-slash-costs/">here</a>.)</div><div class="list-lander-p"></div><div class="list-lander-p">Artificial intelligence companies (whether apps or model makers) typically rely on expensive silicon chips and energy-intensive data centers for computing power to train and run their models and applications. That’s been advantageous for a cohort of infrastructure providers like $2.8 billion-valued Crusoe, $2.5 billion-valued Lambda and $3.3 billion-valued Together AI, which have bubbled up to sate AI’s voracious appetite for compute. (See our deep dive on <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/christopherhelman/2025/04/10/meet-the-tiny-startup-building-stargate-openais-500-billion-data-center-moonshot/">Crusoe</a>.) </div><div class="list-lander-p"></div><div class="list-lander-p">But as companies spend billions of dollars on computing power to train ever larger, more capable models, startups like <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2025/01/30/no-deepseek-is-not-a-sputnik-moment/">Chinese dark horse DeepSeek</a> have shown that training can be done in a more cost efficient way. While DeepSeek isn’t on the AI 50 list this year because the company’s funding, revenues and business practices are opaque, you’ll find a cohort of Chinese AI companies to watch <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/richardnieva/2025/04/10/these-chinese-ai-companies-could-be-the-next-deepseek/">here</a>. </div><div class="list-lander-p"></div><div class="list-lander-p">Some of these startups are grappling with industry-wide issues, one of the biggest being litigation over alleged copyright infringement that is still moving through the courts. Multiple startups on the list, including OpenAI and Anthropic, have been sued for allegedly training their AI models on millions of copyrighted works of art and intellectual property. Meanwhile, a growing group of publishers, artists, musicians and authors have expressed concerns that AI companies have illegally scraped their data from the internet to create tools that then compete with them, posing a threat to their livelihoods. Image and video generation tools like Runway and Midjourney were similarly sued by a group of artists in 2023. Elevenlabs, which develops AI tools to create cloned voices, has faced lawsuits from voice actors. Music generator Suno has faced copyright infringement-related legal action from major record labels for its music generation technology. Cohere and Perplexity have been met with criticism and legal action from a flurry of news publishers for alleged copyright infringement. Forbes sent a cease-and-desist letter to Perplexity in June 2024, <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/sarahemerson/2024/06/07/buzzy-ai-search-engine-perplexity-is-directly-ripping-off-content-from-news-outlets/">accusing it of infringing copyright</a> and joined a class action lawsuit against Cohere in February for similar reasons. AI companies have broadly argued that their use of publicly available copyrighted content falls under fair use. But the future of AI ultimately hinges on court rulings on these suits.    </div><div class="list-lander-p"></div><div class="list-lander-p">This year was among the most competitive for the AI 50 list. Forbes received some 1,860 submissions. Applicants do not pay a fee to be considered and are judged for their business promise, technical talent and use of AI through a quantitative algorithm and qualitative judging panels. Companies are encouraged to share data on diversity, and our list aims to promote a more equitable startup ecosystem. For more, see our full package of coverage, including a detailed explanation of the list methodology, videos and analyses on trends in AI.</div><div class="list-lander-p"></div><div than two years after <a href=\"https://www.forbes.com/sites/alexkonrad/2023/02/02/inside-chatggpts-breakout-moment-and-the-race-for-the-future-of-ai\">the blockbuster launch of ChatGPT</a>, artificial intelligence continues to be the white hot center of venture capital and the business world at large. Some of the buzziest startups have shifted focus from the AI model release horserace to building useful applications and products on top of existing models, automating scutwork across fields like engineering, healthcare, legal and sales. That’s evident in <i>Forbes’</i> seventh annual AI 50 list, produced in partnership with Sequoia and Meritech Capital, which spotlights the most promising privately-held AI companies in the world.   \r\n\r\nNewcomers to the list include $2.5 billion-valued <a href=\"https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2024/08/22/engineers-at-openai-and-midjourney-are-using-this-400-million-startups-ai-coding-software/\">Anysphere</a> (better known as Cursor), a three year-old AI startup that helps engineers write and edit code and has at least $100 million in annualized revenue; the $1 billion-valued AI language tutor app Speak, which is used by some 10 million people to learn English and Spanish; and Massachusetts-based unicorn OpenEvidence, which is building an AI-powered search platform that summarizes medical information for doctors. \r\n\r\nModel builders like OpenAI and Anthropic remain the biggest companies on the list, having raised large sums of cash from marquee Silicon Valley venture capitalists. The two AI behemoths have accumulated a combined $81 billion in venture funding, more than half of the total $142.45 billion that companies on this year’s AI 50 list have raised. But this year, there’s also a hefty new competition from Elon Musk’s xAI ($12.1 billion in funding) and former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati’s stealthy startup Thinking Machine Labs, which is developing broadly capable  AI systems and <a href=\"https://www.businessinsider.com/mira-murati-new-startup-thinking-machine-labs-valuation-2025-2\">reportedly</a> raising $1 billion at a valuation of about $9 billion. Meanwhile, Fei Fei Li, known as the “godmother of AI”, has launched her own startup too, World Labs ($291.5 million raised), to develop models that can understand physical spaces. And then there’s enterprise AI company Writer ($326 million raised), which is training its own models to handle mundane business tasks like writing marketing blogs and searching through troves of documents. (Read our feature story on Writer <a href=\"https://www.forbes.com/sites/rashishrivastava/2025/04/10/why-300-companies-use-this-startups-ai-to-slash-costs/\">here</a>.)\r\n\r\nArtificial intelligence companies (whether apps or model makers) typically rely on expensive silicon chips and energy-intensive data centers for computing power to train and run their models and applications. That’s been advantageous for a cohort of infrastructure providers like $2.8 billion-valued Crusoe, $2.5 billion-valued Lambda and $3.3 billion-valued Together AI, which have bubbled up to sate AI’s voracious appetite for compute. The competition is fierce, pitting the eight-year-old startup against both legacy players like Nvidia as well as rival startups like Groq and Cerebras. SambaNova's edge comes from its focus on combining software with hardware to develop products focused specifically on AI computations and data processing for companies like Aramco, Softbank and Hugging Face. It helps that the company's cofounders include Stanford professors CTO Kunle Olukotun and Christopher Ré, along with CEO Rodrigo Liang, a former longtime senior vice president at Oracle. Since they founded SambaNova in 2017 it has raised $1.1 billion in investment from backers like Accel, OpenAI and Khosla Ventures and is valued at $5.1 billion.","organizationName":"SambaNova","industry":"AI chipmaker","country":"United States","city":"Palo Alto","yearFounded":2017,"funding":1100},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/117278","uri":"scale-ai","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/scale-ai_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"Scale AI was conceived in 2016 as a one-stop shop for supplying human labor to perform tasks that could not be done by algorithms — essentially, the antithesis of AI. Cofounders Alexandr Wang and Lucy Guo had realized humans were vital in labeling the data needed to train the AI used in self-driving cars. Scale capitalized on that boom, setting itself up as a crucial data supplier for generative AI. Nearly a decade later, it works with customers like Meta, Microsoft and OpenAI on labeling training data and building infrastructure for their models. It was last valued at $13.8 billion in May after closing a $1 billion series F funding round backed by Accel, Amazon, Meta and others, cementing Wang's status as one of the world's youngest billionaires at age 28. In March, Scale AI announced a contract with the Department of Defense called Thunderforge to help it use AI for military planning and operations. ","organizationName":"Scale AI","industry":"Data labeling and AI infrastructure","country":"United States","city":"San Francisco","yearFounded":2016,"funding":1600},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/130073","uri":"sierra","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/sierra_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"Sierra is the latest act for its CEO Bret Taylor, the OpenAI board member who was formerly Facebook CTO, Salesforce co-CEO and Twitter chairman. He started the company in 2023 with longtime Google veteran Clay Bavor with the belief that ChatGPT-style conversational AI agents would transform customer service and all the other ways businesses interact with their customers. Sierra's bots are in use at clients like Sonos and SiriusXM and have helped Taylor and Bavor to raise $285 million from top VC firms Benchmark and Sequoia, reaching a $4.5 billion valuation in October 2024.\n","organizationName":"Sierra","industry":"Customer service software","country":"United States","city":"San Francisco","yearFounded":2023,"funding":285},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/134330","uri":"skild-ai","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/skild-ai_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"Founded by former Carnegie Mellon University professors Abhinav Gupta and Deepak Pathak, Skild AI is building a one-size-fits-all AI model that can be slotted into robots of different shapes and sizes. The $1.5 billion-valued startup's secret sauce is training its AI model with 1000 times more data than its rivals, cofounders Gupta and Pathak claim. Even though the company has said little about who its customers are, it has picked up $300 million in venture funding from top investors including Lightspeed Ventures, Coatue and billionaire Jeff Bezos.","organizationName":"Skild AI","industry":"AI systems for robotics","country":"United States","city":"Pittsburgh ","yearFounded":2023,"funding":320},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/124742","uri":"snorkel-ai","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/snorkel-ai_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"Born out of Stanford University's Artificial Intelligence Lab in 2019, Snorkel AI sells software products that allow businesses to annotate, fine-tune and label their data. The company reached a valuation of more than $1 billion after picking up $85 million in a  series C in 2021, bringing its total investment to over $135 million. The company's tools have become a go-to for large companies like Google and furniture retailer Wayfair as well as several of the biggest American banks. In October 2024, the company added a slew of new capabilities for one of its flagship products, Snorkel Flow, including tools to assess the performance of an LLM and more easily extract information from PDFs.  \n","organizationName":"Snorkel AI","industry":"Enterprise data labelling","country":"United States","city":"Redwood City","yearFounded":2019,"funding":135},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/134331","uri":"speak","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/speak_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"It's nearly impossible to truly master a language without human interaction or in-person tutoring. Speak wants to change that by offering an AI tutor for users to converse with, helping them achieve fluency in English and Spanish. In December of 2024, its valuation doubled to $1 billion, after raising $78 million from OpenAI, Khosla Ventures and Y Combinator. Its founders are certainly fluent in entrepreneurship: CEO Connor Zwick previously founded video game company Coco Controller as a Harvard dropout-turned-member of the Thiel Fellowship. That was after starting online learning tool Flashcards+, which education firm Chegg acquired in 2013. Speak cofounder and CTO Andrew Hsu also dropped out of his Stanford neuroscience PhD program to be an inaugural member of the Thiel Fellowship and pursue his ed-tech startup Airy Labs.","organizationName":"Speak","industry":"AI language tutor","country":"United States","city":"San Francisco","yearFounded":2016,"funding":162},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/134332","uri":"stackblitz","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/stackblitz_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"Web development startup StackBlitz was on the verge of shuttering when it found overnight success with Bolt.new, a website-building service that integrates Anthropic's AI models to quickly spin up web pages and apps. The company claims it reached $4 million in annualized revenue within four weeks of launching in October 2024. Bolt has since expanded to offer a tool that can turn a website into a mobile app without any coding.  It raised a series B in January from VC outfits including Emergence Capital and GV (Google Ventures), which brought its total funding to $105 million and boosted it to a $700 million valuation. ","organizationName":"StackBlitz","industry":"Web and mobile app development","country":"United States","city":"San Francisco","yearFounded":2017,"funding":106},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/134333","uri":"suno","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/suno_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"Even Suno admits its technology could be a threat to the status quo of the music industry. The AI music and sound generation startup has caused a stir since its founding in 2022 by CEO Mikey Shulman—a self-described “former mediocre musician,” MIT lecturer and former head of machine learning at S&P Global subsidiary Kensho. Suno uses artificial intelligence to let users create full songs with lyrics and background music from basic text-based prompts. In June, major record labels including Sony and Warner sued the startup for allegedly copying thousands of their songs to train its AI models. The music generator has surprisingly admitted its software is trained on all the music files openly available on the internet, arguing that doing so is fair use. But the legal snafu hasn't dampened investors' interest. The Cambridge-based startup has scooped up $125 million in funding from investors like Lightspeed Venture Partners and GitHub CEO Nat Friedman and has grown to around 12 million users. Valued at $500 million, per Pitchbook, Suno integrated with Amazon's Alexa earlier this year. ","organizationName":"Suno","industry":"Music and sound generation","country":"United States","city":"Cambridge","yearFounded":2022,"funding":125},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/124909","uri":"synthesia","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/synthesia_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"To create videos in 140 languages, simply write a script, pick from one of 230 synthetic avatars and voila! Instavideo. Founded in 2017 by a team of academics and entrepreneurs, Synthesia's generative AI tools are used to create corporate marketing materials as well as influencers' TikTok videos. Big outfits like Reuters and Accenture are among its 65,000 clients. In January, Synthesia landed an additional $180 million in funding and nabbed a $2 billion valuation. CEO Victor Riparbelli—an alumnus of the Forbes 30 Under 30 list—says Synthesia's tech still has room to grow and its avatars could become more realistic. Most recently, Synthesia started selling company shares to actors in exchange for their likenesses, which would be used to create digital avatars. \n\n","organizationName":"Synthesia","industry":"AI avatar and video generator","country":"United Kingdom","city":"London","yearFounded":2017,"funding":330},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/134334","uri":"thinking-machine-labs","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/thinking-machine-labs_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"When OpenAI ousted Sam Altman as CEO two years ago, then-CTO Mira Murati stepped in as interim chief. Her tenure ended four days later, before Altman returned to the company. But now Murati is a CEO again, this time at her own stealthy startup. The firm is coy about what it's working on beyond a focus on science and programming AI. Even minus specifics, the buzz is deafening thanks almost entirely to Murati's reputation: Without revenue, without a product, without a fully defined category, it's said to be planning to raise $1 billion at a valuation of around $9 billion.\n\n","organizationName":"Thinking Machine Labs","industry":"AI research company","country":"United States","city":"San Francisco","yearFounded":2024,"funding":0},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/130074","uri":"together-ai","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/together-ai_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"San Francisco-based Together AI provides cloud computing services and software to 500,000 AI developers and enterprises like Zoom and Quora to train, fine tune and run AI models. The company is also a staunch advocate for open-source AI technology and hosts 200 open source models for video, image and text generation. Since its founding in 2022, it's become one of the largest resources for open source data to train large language models, thanks to its dataset named RedPajama-V2 that contains more than 30 trillion units of data. The company reached a valuation of $3.3 billion after closing a $305 million round led by General Catalyst in February.","organizationName":"Together AI","industry":"AI cloud provider","country":"United States","city":"San Francisco","yearFounded":2022,"funding":534},{"naturalId":"fred/companies/AI/2025/124913","uri":"vannevar-labs","image":"http://images.forbes.com/media/lists/companies/vannevar-labs_416x416.jpg","imageExists":false,"description":"CEO and cofounder Brett Granberg has described Vannevar Labs as the creator of the tools that will deter the next great conflict. Granberg, who previously worked with the CIA's venture arm, has spent the past six years building the startup into a go-to for national security operations, alongside cofounder Nini Moorhead, a former counterterrorism intelligence officer. Today, Vannevar Labs' artificial intelligence software Decrypt reaches military bases globally, where it is used to analyze documents, translate information and find patterns in battlefield information. The U.S. Air Force, for instance, is using it to analyze technical documents about Russia's anti-aircraft systems.
